sentences.text: Check-in acceptance begins when staff confirm that the bag is eligible for carriage under the applicable airline rules.
Staff verify the passenger and flight details before accepting the bag into the checked-baggage process.
The Pier 4 Bag-Drop Unit records the accepted bag and initiates its processing.
The Bag Tag Printer produces a durable tag with a unique identifier for each accepted bag.
The tag identifier is associated with the passenger and flight record in the Baggage Control System.
The Baggage Control System checks that the flight is open for bag acceptance and that the bag record is complete.
Bags with missing, unreadable, or conflicting acceptance data are held for staff resolution before induction.
Staff check bag dimensions and weight against the configured limits for standard conveyor handling.
The Pier 4 Bag-Drop Unit sends an Oversize Exception Ticket when a checked bag exceeds the configured size envelope.
Oversized bags remain in a designated holding area until staff confirm an approved handling route.
The Transfer Bag Feeder identifies each inbound transfer bag and records its arrival into the local handling process.
The Transfer Bag Feeder sends a Late Transfer Bag Card when a bag enters from an inbound transfer stream.
Staff confirm that transfer-bag identifiers are legible and correspond to a valid onward flight record.
The Baggage Control System compares transfer-bag data with the current routing information before the bag is released for induction.
The Flight Data Gateway supplies flight and routing records used for acceptance and induction decisions.
Before induction, the bag record must be valid, the selected route must be available, and the receiving equipment must be ready.
The Concourse Zone Controller grants an induction permissive only when local equipment status and operating restrictions allow movement.
The Induction Tray Conveyor accepts bags through controlled feed points and maintains separation between successive bags.
Interlocks stop feed movement when a jam, access-door opening, or loss of downstream readiness is detected.
The North Gate Scanner reads the bag identifier as the bag enters the screening and sorting network.
The North Gate Scanner is also known locally as Kestrel.
The South Gate Scanner provides an independent read point for bags routed through its assigned entry path.
The Primary Crossbelt Sorter receives inducted bags and directs them according to the active routing data.
The Primary Crossbelt Sorter is also known locally as Juniper.
When automated image review cannot resolve a bag image, staff at the Image Resolution Desk assess the available image and record a disposition.
The Airline Ramp Coordinator sends a Carousel Release Slip when the outbound build is authorized.
